how-much-to-charge-for-a-food-truck-cate.text:
← Food truck event & catering margin calculator

How much to charge for a food truck catering or event booking

Most food truck pricing advice answers a question nobody can use: what other trucks charge per head. The number that decides whether a booking is worth taking is what this booking costs you — and that figure is larger than it looks, for two reasons a per-head price never mentions.

Open the free quote calculator

A 4-hour service window is 8 hours 40 minutes of your day

The hours the client sees are the hours the truck is actually serving. The hours you and your staff commit are longer:

Committed timeMinutes
Service (the hours the client books)240
Commissary prep — portion, pack, and load the menu180
Breakdown — clean and load out60
Round-trip drive40
Total committed per staff member520 (8 hours 40 minutes)

That is 8 hours on site and 8.67 hours committed against 4 hours of visible service. An operator pricing on the service window alone is pricing away more than half the day the booking actually consumes — which is why a fully booked festival weekend can still fail to pay.

Worked example: pricing one booking

A 100-guest Saturday event, two staff at a $22/hour target rate, 30 round-trip miles at $0.67, $4.50 food cost per guest, $25 of propane and generator fuel, a $30 commissary fee, $40 of amortized truck and equipment cost, a $25 special-event permit fee, a 10% peak-day premium on labor and travel, 8% overhead, and a 30% target margin:

LineAmount
Labor (8.67 committed hours × 2 staff × $22)$381.33
Mileage (30 × $0.67)$20.10
Peak-day premium (10% of labor and travel)$40.14
Food (100 guests × $4.50)$450.00
Propane & fuel, commissary fee, truck & equipment, permit$120.00
Direct cost$1,011.58
Overhead (8%)$44.93
Total cost — your break-even$1,056.50
Price at a 30% margin$1,509.29
Profit$452.79
Profit per committed hour$52.24

Note the two per-guest figures this produces. The price works out to $15.09 per guest, which is the number that appears on a competitor's flyer. The profit is $52.24 per committed hour, which is the number that tells you whether the Saturday was worth giving up.

The turnout trap

The quote above assumes 100 guests. Nothing in it obliges the event to cooperate. Run the same booking at 150 guests — a well-attended wedding rather than a guaranteed corporate headcount — and only the food line moves:

Line100 guests150 guests
Food cost$450.00$675.00
Total cost$1,056.50$1,281.50
Price charged$1,509.29$1,509.29
Profit$452.79$227.79

The price never moved and the profit fell by half. This is the structural problem with a flat per-event price built on an expected headcount: the busiest, most successful, most-referred events are the expensive ones to serve, and the quote rewards you the same either way. The calculator flags this as a turnout risk once food cost passes about a third of the price, which is roughly where a normal event-to-event swing starts costing more than the margin can absorb.

There are two honest fixes and one bad habit. Cap the guaranteed guest count, or charge a set rate per guest above it, and the variable cost sits with whoever controls the guest list. Or quote from a realistic high-turnout estimate rather than an average, giving up some quiet-event margin to never be caught out. The bad habit is quoting the optimistic headcount and hoping, because the events most likely to run over are exactly the ones you most wanted to win.

The four costs most often left out

Commissary prep and breakdown time, because it does not feel like the job the client is paying for. Drive time, which is committed labor and not merely fuel — mileage covers the vehicle, not the hour of your life. Truck and equipment amortization, because the truck was bought once and therefore feels free per event, when it is a replacement cost spread over the bookings it will serve. And the one-off special-event permit fee many jurisdictions require on top of the truck's standing license, which a regular route stop never needs.

Common questions

How much should I charge for a food truck catering or event booking?

Price the hours you actually commit, not just the service window. Add commissary prep and breakdown time plus round-trip drive time to your service hours, cost that whole block at what you need to pay staff per hour, then add mileage, food cost for the guest count you expect, propane, the commissary fee, amortized truck and equipment cost, the special-event permit fee, a peak-day premium if it applies, and overhead. Divide the resulting cost by one minus your target margin. In the worked example on this page a 100-guest booking works out to 8 hours 40 minutes of committed time per staff member, costs $1,056.50 all in, and needs a price of $1,509.29 to leave a 30 percent margin.

Why does prep time count when the client only sees the truck serving?

Because you and your staff are committed to the job well before service starts. Commissary prep to portion and pack the menu, the drive to the venue, and breakdown afterward are all real hours a flat per-head price does not show unless you add them in. In the worked example, 3 hours of prep, 4 hours of service, and 1 hour of breakdown plus a 40-minute round-trip drive add up to 8 hours 40 minutes of committed time against 4 hours of visible service.

How does turnout risk affect a flat-price food truck quote?

A flat per-event quote is built from an expected or guaranteed guest count, but food cost scales with how many people actually get served, and a well-attended wedding or a festival with a longer line can serve far more guests than a corporate lunch headcount. In the worked example, quoting $1,509.29 on an expected 100 guests leaves $452.79 of profit; if turnout runs to 150 guests, food cost rises from $450.00 to $675.00 and the total cost rises to $1,281.50, so the profit at the same quoted price falls to $227.79. The price never moved and the profit dropped by half.

Should I cap the guest count or price for the busy case?

Either works as long as you choose deliberately. Capping the guaranteed count, or charging a set rate per guest above it, keeps the variable cost with the person who controls the guest list. Pricing for the busy case means quoting off a realistic high turnout estimate rather than an average one, which costs some quiet-event margin in exchange for never being caught out. What does not work is quoting off an optimistic headcount and hoping, because the events most likely to run over are the large, well-referred ones you most wanted to win.

What costs do food truck operators most often leave out of an event quote?

Four, in roughly this order. Commissary prep and breakdown time, because it does not feel like the job the client is paying for. Round-trip drive time, which is committed labor and not only fuel. Truck and equipment amortization, because the truck was bought once and so feels free per event, when it is really a replacement cost spread across the bookings it will serve. And the one-off special-event or temporary health permit fee many jurisdictions require on top of the truck's standing license, which a regular route stop never needs.

Run it on your own booking

The calculator takes every figure used above, reports your break-even and target price, shows profit per committed hour, and flags the turnout risk before you send the quote. It runs entirely in your browser.

A per-head price isn't the whole quote.

A "$8/head, 100-guest minimum" quote prices the food but usually leaves out commissary prep time, the drive to the venue, propane, the one-off special-event permit, and the risk that a better turnout than expected quietly eats the margin. Common questions

Why does a per-head quote need to count prep and travel time at all?

Because the truck and its staff are committed to the job well before service starts. Commissary prep, the drive to the venue, and breakdown afterward are real hours that a flat "$8/head" price does not show unless you add them in — and they happen whether the event runs 2 hours or 6.

Why does the calculator treat turnout as a risk, not just a cost line?

A flat per-event quote is built from an expected or guaranteed guest count, but actual turnout depends on the event — a well-attended wedding or a festival with a longer line can serve far more guests than a corporate lunch headcount. The calculator reports what share of your price the food line already represents, so you can see how much room is left before a bigger-than-expected crowd erases the margin you built the quote on.

How is the recommended extra-guest rate different from just charging my per-head food cost for the extra seats?

It marks the extra guest's food cost up the same way the rest of the quote is marked up — food cost plus your overhead rate, divided by your target margin — so seats added the week before an event still earn the same margin instead of just covering the added food at cost.

Does anything about my event details get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only, there is no account, and nothing you type is uploaded. Nothing leaves this device unless you choose to send it: the Copy shareable link button puts the quote on the form into the page's URL fragment, which a browser never sends to a server or into a Referer header, so it reaches only the person you hand the link to. Anyone who has that link can read the quote in it, so send it the way you would send the numbers themselves. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above.

vs-a-flat-per-guest-price.html.text:
← Food truck event & catering margin calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-guest price

“$15 a guest” sounds like a rate. It is really one booking's price, divided by that booking's own headcount, offered up as if it applied to the next one too.

Open the free quote calculator

What a flat per-guest price is

Dividing a quote by its guest count is the fastest way to compare two bookings, and the fastest way to quote a new one: take the figure that worked last time and multiply by the new headcount. It travels well — a client can repeat a $/guest number back to you from a competitor's flyer — which is exactly why it gets applied to bookings it was never built for.

The number was set for one booking's own prep time, drive, and permit requirements, and then reused for every booking after, whether or not the next one shares any of them.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter each booking's own commissary prep, service, and breakdown hours, round-trip drive time and mileage, staffing, food cost per guest, fuel, commissary fee, amortized truck and equipment cost, and the special-event permit fee — then it returns the break-even cost and a bid price above your target margin for this booking, not a rate carried over from the last one.

What a flat per-guest price doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/guest whether the venue is 15 minutes away or over an hour, even though every extra mile and minute is committed staff time a headcount never counts.Prices round-trip drive time as committed labor for every staff member on the job, so a farther venue costs more than a close one of the same size.
Has no line for a booking's own special-event permit, whether it needs the truck's standing license alone or its own added fee on top.Prices the permit fee per booking, so a job that needs its own permit costs more than one that doesn't.
Divides the same fixed commissary prep, breakdown, commissary fee, and equipment amortization by whatever headcount a booking happens to have, so a small booking is charged as if those costs shrank with it.Charges commissary prep, breakdown, the commissary fee, and equipment amortization once per booking regardless of headcount, so a small booking isn't quietly undercharged for them.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against.Reports the break-even cost and the dollar gap against a flat per-guest rate, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two bookings, the same headcount-blind rate

Using this calculator's own defaults for the first booking ($22/hr staff wage, $0.67/mile, $4.50 food cost per guest, $25 propane and generator fuel, a $30 commissary fee, $40 of amortized truck and equipment cost, a $25 permit fee, a 10% peak-day premium, 8% overhead, a 30% target margin):

BookingThis calculator's priceThe flat $15.09/guest rateGap
100 guests, 40-minute round trip, 30 miles, $25 permit — the booking the rate is set from$1,509.29 bid price; $1,056.50 break-even cost$1,509.29 (exactly $15.09/guest — this rate is fit to this booking)No gap on the booking the rate was built on.
40 guests, 2-hour-30-minute round trip, 120 miles, $6.00 food cost per guest, its own $75 event permit$1,525.67 bid price; $1,067.97 break-even cost$603.72The rate quotes $464.26 below this booking's own break-even cost — before a dollar of profit — and $921.96 below the calculator's own bid price.

Fewer guests, further from break-even. The second booking has less than half the headcount of the first, yet costs more to run: labor rises from $381.33 to $462.00 (10 hours 30 minutes committed per staff member instead of 8 hours 40 minutes), mileage rises from $20.10 to $80.40, and the permit fee triples from $25 to $75. None of that shows up in a rate measured only in dollars per guest.

Common questions

Why is a flat price per guest the wrong way to quote a food truck booking?

Because it is not actually a rate for a guest — it is one booking's total price divided by that booking's own headcount, then reused on a different booking as if it were a market rate. Commissary prep, travel time, truck and equipment amortization, and the one-off special-event permit fee do not scale with guest count, so a per-guest number set from one booking silently drops all of them when applied to a smaller or farther one.

How big is the gap in practice?

On this calculator's own defaults, a 100-guest booking 15 minutes from the commissary prices at $1,509.29, or $15.09 a guest. Apply that same $15.09 a guest to a 40-guest private booking 1 hour 15 minutes away that needs its own $75 event permit, and the flat rate quotes $603.72 — $464.26 below that smaller booking's own $1,067.97 break-even cost, before a dollar of profit, and $921.96 below the calculator's own $1,525.67 price.

Why does the smaller booking cost more per guest, not less?

Because most of a booking's cost does not depend on the guest count at all. Commissary prep and breakdown, the drive, the commissary fee, truck and equipment amortization, and the permit fee are paid once per booking whichever way the headcount falls, so a booking with fewer guests spreads that same fixed cost over fewer heads — and a farther venue and its own permit requirement add to that fixed cost rather than shrinking it.

Is a per-guest rate ever a reasonable shorthand?

For quickly comparing two bookings of similar size, similar distance, and similar scope, a per-guest figure can be close enough to sanity-check against. The risk is carrying that number to a booking that differs on drive time, headcount, or permit needs without re-deriving it — at which point it is no longer describing the booking in front of you, only the one it was set from.

Does this calculator know what a per-guest rate should be in my market?

No. It has no data on what other trucks charge and makes no claim about local pricing norms. It takes your own prep, service, and breakdown hours, drive time and mileage, staffing, food cost, fuel, commissary fee, equipment amortization, and permit fee, and turns them into a price for the booking you describe — the arithmetic a flat per-guest rate skips, not a market survey.

← Food truck event margin calculator

This calculator vs. Roaming Hunger

Roaming Hunger is a food truck catering marketplace: an event planner submits a request, Roaming Hunger sends it to trucks in the area, and available trucks submit a catering package with their own pricing. Most of that bidding is free and a truck keeps its full bid, but for a guaranteed, contracted booking Roaming Hunger facilitates directly, it charges a vendor fee and holds the funds until after the event.

That makes Roaming Hunger the right choice for finding a booking you don't already have. This page answers a narrower, faster question: for a booking you already have — a lead you found yourself, a planner who called you directly, a returning client — what should you actually charge, free, with no listing and nothing taken out of the price you set.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I don't have a booking yet — where do I find one? Roaming Hunger's marketplace, or another lead source.
I already have a booking (or a lead) — what should I quote them? This calculator — enter your numbers, get a price immediately, nothing listed.
Does my quote actually cover prep, travel, and breakdown time, not just the food? This calculator — see how much to charge for a catering event.
How much room does this quote have before a bigger-than-expected turnout erases the margin? This calculator's turnout-risk warning — flags when food cost share gets tight.
Can I get an answer without listing my truck or paying a vendor fee? This calculator — a static page, no sign-up, no fee.
Price your booking now

This tool needs no account and lists nothing: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and your guest count, costs, and every other figure stay on this device — nothing is uploaded anywhere, there is no marketplace listing, and no fee on whatever you and your client agree to.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Roaming Hunger?

They solve different problems. Roaming Hunger is a marketplace: an event planner submits a request, Roaming Hunger sends it to food trucks in the area, and trucks that want the job submit a catering package with their own pricing — for a guaranteed, contracted booking, Roaming Hunger can facilitate the deal directly for a vendor fee, and it holds the funds until after the event. This page is a free calculator: no listing, no lead generation, no vendor fee. You already have the booking, or a lead you found yourself, and you type your guest count, food cost, prep and travel time, staff labor, and other costs, and it prices what that specific job needs to charge to hit your target margin.

Does Roaming Hunger charge the same way this calculator prices a booking?

Not really comparable — they solve different problems. Roaming Hunger's own guidance says most catering leads are free to bid on and a truck keeps its full bid with no deduction, but some events run on a revenue-share or vendor-fee model, particularly a guaranteed, contracted booking it facilitates directly, and it does not publish one fixed commission rate. This calculator doesn't take a cut of anything; it prices a booking from your own prep hours, travel, staff labor, propane, permit fee, and target margin, independent of whatever price Roaming Hunger's marketplace happened to yield for someone else's truck.

Is Roaming Hunger free?

Getting listed and receiving leads is free, and most catering work carries no commission — you bid what you want and keep it. But for a guaranteed, contracted booking Roaming Hunger facilitates directly, it charges a vendor fee, and it holds the funds until after the event rather than paying you up front. This calculator has no listing, no lead flow, and nothing that bills — it is a free static page with no server behind the numbers you type.
